# A note is an atomic step relative to the check that reads it

A knowledge base written and reviewed by agents bounds note size twice, for two
reasons that have nothing to do with each other.

The first bound is co-loading. [Short composable notes maximize combinatorial
discovery](./short-composable-notes-maximize-combinatorial-discovery.md)
because a model's context is finite, so the number of notes that fit in it
together sets the surface area for recognizing shared structure. One claim per
note, sized to the reader's context.

The second bound is checking. A note is an **atomic step** when the claim, the
material it cites, and the inference from that material to the claim can be
checked in one pass by the check that will be applied to it. One checkable
inference, sized to the checker's pass.

These are different quantities set by different mechanisms, and a note can
satisfy one and fail the other. "Fits one pass" also has no content until the
pass is named: a step is atomic relative to a particular check, which is an
instance of the general rule that [warranted autonomy is bounded by oracle
domain](./warranted-autonomy-is-bounded-by-oracle-domain.md) — a checker's
domain is the range of candidates it can assess with the required confidence,
and [the boundary of automation is the boundary of
verification](./the-boundary-of-automation-is-the-boundary-of-verification.md).
The same note may be one step for a check that judges whether quoted passages
support a claim and several steps for a check that judges whether an inference
across all of them holds. This note states the rule for one check, Commonplace's
grounding check, because that is where the unit of cost is clear; the same
argument would need its own unit for any other check.

## Placing the bound on the artifact rather than the review

The alternative placement is a reading budget on the review: let notes be as
large as they are, and calibrate how much the reviewer may open. The two
placements differ in their failure mode, not in the constraint they express.

A review-side budget has to be recalibrated whenever the corpus's evidence needs
move, and its failure when it lags is silent. A reviewer that stops at its limit
and returns a pass is indistinguishable, from the outside, from one that read
everything and returned a pass. Disclosure conventions reduce this — a reviewer
can name what it left unread — but disclosure reports the budget's boundary, not
whether a finding was sitting behind it.

An artifact-side bound does not have that failure mode, because a conforming
artifact fits by construction: the bound is held by a validator that fails the
note, not by a reviewer that stops reading. The reviewer's limit still exists;
on a conforming note it never binds.

## Mechanism: for the grounding check, the unit is the unquoted source

The grounding check asks whether the material a note cites supports the claim it
is cited for. Its cost is not links, and not bytes: it is the number of
artifacts in which the reviewer must *find* the passage that carries the claim
and then judge whether it does. A source that has been quoted verbatim is not
one of them.

The reason is that Commonplace has moved that finding step into code. A
quotation marked `verbatim` is resolved by substring match against the file it
links, and a mismatch fails the note before any reviewer opens anything ([ADR
046](../reference/adr/046-verbatim-quotes-are-validated-against-their-cited-source.md));
the source-side material is itself held as retained quotes validated against the
captured source ([ADR
073](../reference/adr/073-untracked-source-snapshots-require-ingest-grounding.md)).
This is the general rule that [a derived copy of recomputable truth must be
checked or absent](./a-derived-copy-of-recomputable-truth-must-be-checked-or-absent.md)
applied to citation: the quote is a copy of something held elsewhere, and it is
admissible because a validator re-derives it and fails on mismatch. A paraphrase
has no such derivation rule, and [a citation cannot assert more fidelity than
its capture preserved](./a-citation-cannot-assert-more-fidelity-than-its-capture-preserved.md)
— a passage never captured word for word cannot be quoted into this route
without returning to the source.

What is left for the reviewer after the quote is a bounded judgment: does *this
passage* support *this claim*. It costs attention, and nine quoted passages cost
more than one, but the cost is set by the author's choice of passage length and
requires opening nothing.

Two limits follow, and both are prices already paid elsewhere in the system.
Occurrence is not representativeness: the validator establishes that the words
appear in the source, not that they mean there what the note uses them for, and
a reader who suspects a passage was lifted out of a qualifying context has to
open the source after all. And some claims cannot be carried by a bounded
passage — claims resting on the structure of a whole argument, on what a source
does not say, or on material distributed across a document. Commonplace marks
those uses `(snapshot required)`; such a source has no bounded passage and
counts fully against the step.

A consequence worth stating, because it answers the obvious objection to
bounding the artifact: a claim supported *jointly* by several sources, none
sufficient alone, should be quoted rather than split. Splitting it across notes
severs the support, so each fragment fails a check the whole would pass — the
hazard the review-side proposal *Exceeding a review budget splits the task*,
now archived, identified when it concluded that any partition would have to be
by claim rather than by link. Under an artifact-side bound the author, who knows which passages
jointly carry the claim, puts them on the page together and the check reads them
together. This is where the two bounds meet: every quoted passage lengthens the
note, so quoting spends against the co-loading bound. The bounds are independent
as constraints but coupled through this remedy. A claim whose joint support
cannot be quoted within a note the reader can still co-load has only the
snapshot route or a split left, and the split has to be by claim, so that each
fragment states what it establishes. Links to other notes are also not sources in this sense, because a
linked note carries its own claim title and its own grounding review; [a
linked note discharges its own grounding, so a citing note owes it
representation, not re-grounding](./a-linked-note-discharges-its-own-grounding-so-a-citing-note-owes.md).

## The two bounds come apart in the corpus

Across 344 notes in `kb/notes/` as of 2026-08-27, eight cite more than five
distinct sources, the largest citing nine. All eight are single-claim notes: one
proposition, established or bounded by reading six or more sources together.
They satisfy the co-loading bound on any reading of it. They are not atomic
steps for the grounding check, because checking one means opening six to nine
artifacts and finding the claimed support in each. The converse case is
available in principle — two independent claims, each grounded in one quoted
passage, is one step for the grounding check and two notes under the co-loading
bound.

The strongest evidence Commonplace holds about grounding-review reading limits
reads differently under this placement. A paired experiment reviewed the same
twelve notes under a five-link instruction and an uncapped one; [four findings
appeared only in the uncapped
arm](../reports/retained/a-five-link-cap-missed-four-grounding-findings-in-twelve-reviews.md),
after the reviewer had opened six, eleven, fourteen and sixteen artifacts. Read
as a fact about reviewers, this says five is too few. Read as a fact about
notes, it says the reviewer honoured its cap and the notes had put their support
beyond it — which is the behaviour an artifact-side bound depends on, and under
such a bound the four notes would have had to split or quote before review. Two
of the four findings sharpen the reading: one was missing retained support for
details attributed to a source, and one was an ingest's analytical prose treated
as evidence beyond its retained quotes. Both are absences of a retained passage,
and an absence of that kind is a validator's result rather than a reviewer's
finding. Had the details been quoted, either the quote would match or the note
would have failed validation before review began.

## What kind of number a step size is

The bound does not fix its own N, but it does fix what kind of number N is,
because three candidates are available and they justify different values.

N is not the point at which reviewer performance degrades. In the same
experiment, uncapped reviewers read up to twenty-two artifacts and 322 kilobytes
in one pass with no observed loss, and the three notes offering the most
material all passed. Whatever a small step protects, on this evidence it is not
a reviewer capacity exhausted at current corpus sizes. Nor is N the smallest
count at which no miss happened to be observed; that number moves with every
experiment and inherits its sample.

N is a convention, chosen so that a second checker — including a person — can
redo the step. This is what a small step buys that a well-calibrated reviewer
budget does not. A verdict resting on fourteen artifacts costs as much to audit
as it cost to produce, so in practice it is trusted rather than audited; a
verdict resting on three sources and six quoted passages can be re-checked from
the same page. What the page re-checks is the support judgment — that these
passages carry this claim; whether a passage was lifted out of a qualifying
context still costs a trip to the source, so the audit the bound buys is of the
step the validator did not do, not of the one it cannot. The value is not that
the reviewer copes, but that the review
becomes auditable — and Commonplace's own measurement that language-model
verdicts disagree with themselves on unchanged input is the reason auditability
is worth paying for.

Sizing a step to its checker rather than to the material is old. Descartes'
second precept of method was "to divide each of the difficulties under
examination into as many parts as possible, and as might be necessary for its
adequate solution" ([*Discourse on the Method*, Part
II](../sources/descartes-discourse-on-the-method.ingest.md), verbatim, Veitch's
translation). What he claimed for such division was the reliability of long
chains: "The long chains of simple and easy reasonings by means of which
geometers are accustomed to reach the conclusions of their most difficult
demonstrations" ([Part
II](../sources/descartes-discourse-on-the-method.ingest.md), verbatim) had
persuaded him that anything within reach of knowledge could be reached that way.
The parts are sized to the solution, and the chain is trusted because each link
is simple enough to be evident.

Lamport makes the checker explicit. Asked how much detail a proof step needs, he
answers that when the proof is written to convince someone else "the answer
depends on the sophistication of the reader" ([*How to Write a 21st Century
Proof*, section
3](../sources/lamport-how-to-write-a-21st-century-proof.ingest.md), verbatim).
Written for oneself, the test is different: "if the truth of a statement is not
completely obvious, or if you suspect that there may be just the slightest
possibility that it is not correct, then more detail is needed" ([section
3](../sources/lamport-how-to-write-a-21st-century-proof.ingest.md), verbatim).
That is step size stated relative to whoever checks the step. His assessment of
what the structure delivers is measured: "Structured proofs make it possible,
not inevitable" ([section
5](../sources/lamport-how-to-write-a-21st-century-proof.ingest.md), verbatim).
The same modesty applies here — a bounded check does not catch every error, but
an unbounded one cannot be redone. Both precedents concern human checkers
reading mathematical arguments, so the transfer to agent-reviewed notes is an
analogy about checker-relative sizing, not evidence that any particular N
carries over. What the knowledge-base case adds is a validator that turns the
commonest kind of step — *this passage says this* — into a check that costs the
reviewer nothing.

## Scope

- Stated for Commonplace's grounding check. The relativity claim is general;
  the unit — the unquoted source — is derived from that check's cost structure
  and would have to be re-derived for any other check.
- Depends on a system where verbatim quotations are mechanically validated
  against their cited source. Without that validator, quoting moves work around
  rather than discharging it.
- Does not decide N, a validator rule that would enforce it, or the fate of the
  review-side budget currently in force. Those are operational decisions with
  their own evidence requirements.
- The corpus counts and the paired experiment are bounded local reports about
  one knowledge base at one time; they show the two bounds are independent
  here, not how often they diverge elsewhere.

## Open Questions

- Is the check that a citing note represents a linked note's claim faithfully
  itself well bounded, or is it where the same problem reappears in smaller
  form? One of the four findings was a broader mechanism attributed to a link
  that disclaims it, which no count would catch.
- Does the artifact-side bound have a cost the review-side one avoids — claims
  that are genuinely one inference over many sources and cannot be quoted into
  bounded passages, which would be pushed toward the snapshot route or toward
  fragmentation?

# Revise an article or note

Make the artifact serve the operator's stated purpose without changing what it
claims, by assessing first and then running only the passes the assessment
recommends. This is a planning-containing procedure. When the purpose, scope
and pass are already fixed, use the fixed-plan route in the
[simplification-pass guide](./README.md#fixed-plan-execution-the-simple-baseline)
instead of assessing again.

## Prerequisites

- A purpose in one line: who the reader is and what they should notice or be
  able to do. If the operator named only the artifact, propose the purpose
  at the top of the assessment and proceed under it; the operator corrects
  it if it is wrong.
- The artifact's claims are settled. A claim in dispute goes to the operator
  as a question, not into a pass.

## Steps

1. **Assess before editing.** Read the whole artifact. Report a ranked list
   of changes, highest value against the purpose first, each with its cost
   in one phrase and the pass from this directory that would make it. Name
   the sentence a hostile reviewer would attack first. Say what reads well
   in one sentence. Recommend only passes whose value against the purpose
   is clear; an item you would not defend is not recommended. Do not edit.

   If the highest-value change is a rewrite or a restructuring of the
   argument, report that and stop. The passes work on text, and text a
   rewrite will replace is not worth a pass; recommend passes only over the
   parts the assessment expects to survive.

   When the assessment finds that a claim itself is wrong or unsupported,
   the passes cannot fix it: they do not change claims. Set the plan's
   `stop`, name the claim, and name the rewrite route:
   `commonplace-review run rewrite NOTE --commission FILE`, with the
   commission prepared with `cp-skill-write-multistage`.

   Two things the passes cannot own belong in the assessment too. For each
   candidate overclaim, propose whether the sentence is support (may be
   narrowed) or divergence (must be kept); the divergence items become the
   packets' `Must keep:` line unless the operator objects. And list
   qualifications that have gone stale against the body: a scope bullet
   qualifying words the body no longer uses, a table cell filed under the
   wrong row, a cross-note ordinal pointing at the wrong list. These are
   claim questions for the operator, applied as their own commits after
   approval, not passes.

   Review findings may come with the artifact. Each is a stored review
   result with outcome `warn` or `fail`, and each names its criterion and
   the depth that criterion declares. Read them with the artifact. By
   default, a finding at depth *n* points at the pass at depth *n*. A
   finding whose criterion is named in a pass's `responds-to` may instead
   become a plan entry for that pass, with the result file as the entry's
   `finding`. That entry takes the depth of the finding's criterion in the
   order. [Fix a finding by a named strategy](../fix-warnings/fix-strategy-taxonomy.md)
   is such a pass: it changes only the passage the finding names. Recommend
   the change a finding points at only when its value against the purpose
   is clear. List the findings you do not act on once, each with its reason.

   The operator's decisions on findings of the artifact may come as
   `earlier-decisions`: findings the operator rejected or deferred at a
   triage, each with the operator's reason. Plan no fix for a finding the
   operator rejected unless the text changed in a way that answers the
   operator's reason; say so when you plan one. Plan no fix for a deferred finding unless its
   `revisit` condition is met.

   Depth 1 review reports may come with the artifact as well: critique,
   composition friction and premise decomposition. If one of them proposes
   changing what the artifact is (a split, a merge, a different claim or a
   rejection), set the plan's `stop` and list no passes. The stop names the
   proposal and the repository path of the report it comes from. The run
   then ends with nothing edited, and the operator decides the proposal.
   When the proposal is to move a full argument into a separate file, the
   stop may recommend [split out a treatment](./split-out-a-treatment.md);
   no procedure runs it.

   The [role report](../role-in-the-kb-gate.md) may come as well. It states
   the artifact's role in the KB from the passages that link to it: what
   each dependent needs from it, what it duplicates, and which
   recommendations in linking sources it has not taken up. It does not
   judge whether a claim is good theory: do not plan to cut content
   because no dependent uses it. Read it before
   you stop on a depth 1 proposal or plan around one. Check whether the
   proposal's cause may be a term or claim that dependents rely on: a
   contradiction inside the artifact can come from a term a dependent
   uses in another sense. When the proposed change, or a pass you would
   plan, changes a claim or term that dependents rely on, set `stop` and
   name those dependents in it, with the role report's run directory: the
   passes edit only the artifact, so the operator must decide the
   dependents' change too.

2. **Dispatch each recommended pass as a packet.** Proceed without waiting;
   the report gives the operator the chance to interrupt. Run passes one at a time,
   since they share one write scope. Order them by depth, not by the
   assessment's ranking: a pass whose edits a later pass would rewrite runs
   after it. The order that has held is split-out-a-treatment,
   narrow-overclaims, abstractions, readability-and-flow, plain-wording,
   opening-and-title. Abstractions runs before the structural moves although
   it is a wording pass, because one name per thing is what makes a
   duplicated caveat or two paragraphs on one subject visible; the opening
   runs last because the TL;DR restates a body the earlier passes have
   settled. Make the plain-wording list after the structural moves land; a
   list made against the earlier text names passages that have moved or
   gone. Each pass file carries an `effort`
   field: `simple` passes run in a fresh worker on a cheaper model or lower
   effort; `judgment` passes run on the session model, in the current
   context or a fresh worker. Use a fresh worker when the pass benefits from
   not having seen the conversation, as the plain-wording and
   readability passes do; run narrow-overclaims in the parent context, where
   the conversation is the evidence. Apply one-word swaps and two-sentence
   narrowings in the parent context rather than as packets. Small scoped
   edits from different passes may share one packet when its scope is
   enumerated. The packet is:

   ```
   Purpose: {the operator's one line}
   Artifact: {path}
   Pass: {absolute path of {pass}.md in this instruction's directory}
   Must keep: {what this run keeps beyond the write brief's Must keep; a pass may not narrow it}
   Write scope: {the artifact only | none, return proposals}
   Return: the pass's report, plus items noticed but not applied, nothing committed
   ```

   The worker chooses means within the pass. It does not widen the write
   scope, add claims, or remove evidence.

3. **Integrate.** After each pass read the diff, and read every replaced
   phrase in its full sentence, not in the diff summary; a literal
   replacement can supply a referent the original left implicit and supply
   the wrong one. List each mapping, contrast, example, price, or link the
   diff removed and check that the pass report accounts for it; restore what
   it does not, in the classes [audit-a-prior-pass](./audit-a-prior-pass.md)
   uses. A pass that narrows or tightens a sentence tends to take its
   neighbours with it. Run `commonplace-validate` on the artifact, and commit the
   pass alone with a body saying what it was meant to make true. If the operator reverts part of a pass, record the
   threshold they applied in the pass file or a memory, so the next run
   starts from it.

4. **Stop when the recommended passes are done.** Report what each pass
   changed. Items you assessed but did not recommend, and the not-applied
   items the workers returned, are listed once, not run.

## Run it as a workflow

`commonplace-review run revise ARTIFACT --assess --purpose TEXT [--must-keep CLAIM ...]`
runs these steps with headless workers, which never write the checkout. This
is the quick procedure. The assessment also receives the artifact's fresh
stored review results with outcome `warn` or `fail`, when any exist; the
command launches no review. Results with only INFO-level findings are not
given. A finding the operator rejected at a triage of the same result is
removed, and the operator's rejected and deferred findings of the artifact
come as `earlier-decisions`. The focused procedure makes no assessment: `--pass NAME` runs a
one-entry plan for that pass, and `--finding RESULT` runs a one-entry plan
that fixes that review result of the artifact. The triage, `--triage`, makes
no assessment either: it stops with one answers file per fresh `warn` or
`fail` result, the operator decides each finding with
[decide items](../decide-items.md), and the plan fixes the approved findings
only, one entry per result with an approved finding. The full procedure, `--full`,
first runs every review operation that declares a `depth` on the artifact,
through the same route as `commonplace-review run gates`. Its results go to
the shared store, and fresh results are reused. The compression synthesis
then runs on the compression checks' results, and the role report on the
artifact's inbound contexts; neither publishes a result. The assessment
receives the fresh `warn` and `fail` results, the depth 1 reports, the
synthesis report and the role report. A review that ends without a result stops the run before the
assessment. The full procedure does not review the edited text. Its
run directory is derived from the artifact's path and the hash of its text.
It stops with a proposal wherever this procedure waits for the operator.
Repeating alone never approves the proposal or starts its dependent work.
A repeat reuses the recorded `--purpose`, `--must-keep` and profiles unless you
give them again. Each approval stop prints a JSON report whose `waiting-for` gives
what to do, the file, proposal key, `approve-command` and command to repeat.
Assessment, planning and settled intermediate passes are preauthorized;
never wait for routine plan approval. Each stop's file is a pending
[answers](../../types/answers.md) file: record the operator's decision on its
items before the `approve-command`, then repeat the workflow command.
Approval captures that text; later edits require approval again and are
listed under `unapproved-edits`. Changed proposal inputs require fresh approval. An agent
may approve only on the operator's stated word for that specific proposal;
it must not infer approval from a request to retry. This instruction and the
pass files own judgment; worker prompts name inputs, not additional criteria.

1. Step 1 runs as one assessment ask, on the profile for `judgment`. The run
   retains `assessment.md` and `plan.yaml` under the run directory's
   `artifact/` for inspection and proceeds with the validated plan.
   `--plan FILE` supplies an explicit input or override without assessment
   or approval, including replacement of a stopped plan. The plan holds
   `purpose`, `must-keep`, `passes` in run order (each a `pass` name, an
   optional `scope` and, for a pass that declares `responds-to`, the
   `finding` it fixes) and `stop`. A plan with `stop` set ends the run without
   editing the artifact. To run passes instead, supply a replacement with
   `stop` cleared and the desired passes through `--plan`; editing the
   retained `artifact/plan.yaml` alone is not an override.
   A stopped plan also leaves `artifact/stop-answers.md`, an
   [answers](../../types/answers.md) file with one item for the plan. The
   run does not wait for it; its report names it under `stop-answers`.
   Record the operator's decision on the proposal there: `approved` to act
   on it as made, or `rejected` or `deferred` with the operator's reason.
   When the work that followed is done, add `resolution` (what was done,
   when it differs from or goes beyond the proposal) and `refs` (commit
   hashes, paths, a workshop directory) to the item. Run the reported
   approval command each time the file changes, so that
   `commonplace-review decisions` lists the current text.
   The command rejects a plan that names an unknown pass, misses a field,
   has a field it does not know,
   names a `finding` that is not a review result of the artifact, or breaks
   the depth order the pass files and the findings' criteria declare. A replacement supplied
   with `--plan` reuses calls whose inputs did not change and reruns the others.
2. Step 2 runs each listed pass as one run of the edit route, the same one
   `commonplace-review run edit` uses, on the profile from
   `instructions/review-profiles.yaml` that its `effort` selects. Code checks
   the edit result and the revised text (title, type, brief declaration and
   H1 kept; no new validation failure; link targets and quoted spans kept),
   and the next pass works on that text. Each run's result and candidate are
   retained under `artifact/edits/`. Every pass must end
   `applied`, `no-change` or `skipped` before final publication is offered.
   After a `problem` pass, or while the run waits, the original artifact is
   untouched, and `not-applied` names the run file holding the proposed text.
   The workflow does not commit.
3. A pass whose `decision` is `per-item` (plain-wording, abstractions) first
   returns proposals, and stops with the pending answers file
   `artifact/<pass>-answers-<key>.md`: one item per proposal, holding its
   `quote`, `change` and `reason`, every item `pending`. In a session, follow
   [decide items](../decide-items.md): the agent presents each item in
   context, asks, and records the operator's answer as `approved`,
   `rejected` with a reason, or `deferred` with a reason and a revisit
   condition. Run the stop's approval command, then repeat; the same
   operation runs again with the answers file as its `answers` input and
   applies only the `approved` items. Code refuses a candidate that changed

approved publication. Use this procedure in a
conversation instead when the passes are chosen as the conversation goes,
when a pass needs the conversation as evidence, or when each pass should be
integrated and committed before the next one runs.

## Headless write briefs

When the artifact declares a [write brief](../../types/write-brief.md), the assessment and every pass
(including candidate-list and apply workers) receive its captured text as
`brief`. Pass workers receive [execute a revision pass](./execute-a-revision-pass.md)
as `execution`, not this planning procedure. That execution instruction carries
the pass bounds and brief constraints without commissioning assessment or dispatch.

Treat the supplied brief as binding retained intent. It is the one lasting
statement of what the artifact must keep and exclude. Keep its Must keep,
Must exclude and Reserved decisions in both the plan and the edited text.
Do not amend the brief or remove or change the artifact's `brief:` field.

The plan starts from the brief. Its `must-keep` lists only what this run adds
to the brief's Must keep: the operator's must-keep items and the claims the
assessment marks as divergence. Do not restate the brief's items there; every
pass receives the brief. Never plan a pass that conflicts with the brief.

set the plan's `stop`, list no passes, and name the brief item and the
conflicting text.

A pass worker that finds the purpose, the must-keep list, the validated plan,
an approved candidate list or its instruction in conflict with the brief

or publication approval does not authorise amending the brief. The operator
must resolve the commission change outside this workflow before continuing.

invocations invalidates affected calls and dependent approvals; a change during an
invocation blocks publication. A missing or invalid declared brief stops the
run before workers launch. Supplying it does not mechanically verify that
an edit respects its meaning; the worker must identify conflicts.

- The assessment is one full read. Each pass is one more. Do not re-read
  linked notes unless a pass names them.
- A worker gets the artifact path and the packet, never the conversation.
- Propose-only work (the assessment, the plain-wording list, title
  proposals) may run in parallel; edits to the artifact run in sequence.
- Stop when the recommended passes are done. An item not recommended costs
  nothing; recommending a pass of unclear value costs a read and a diff.

## Verify

- Every applied change traces to a recommended pass.
- Every passage a diff weakened is accounted for by that pass's report.
- No claim, evidence, or qualification changed unless the operator asked.
- Conversational execution validates and commits each integrated pass. The
  headless workflow instead retains per-pass reports and checked texts, then
  permits one final write only after publication approval.
- Operator reverts have been recorded as thresholds.

Second, most of the body develops grounding-check-specific and prescriptive claims (artifact-side placement, the unquoted source as unit, N as an auditability convention). # Friction check: A note is an atomic step relative to the check that reads it

**Central claim (one sentence):** A note's size is bounded both by co-loading and by the check that reads it, so atomicity is check-relative; for Commonplace's grounding check, the unit is the unquoted source, and placing that bound on the artifact rather than the review turns a silent budget failure into a loud validation failure and makes the review auditable.

## Filter
**Filter:** SURVIVES

The properties the claim holds together are two independent bounds, quoting as the remedy for jointly supported claims, and an artifact-side bound with no silent failure. They could conflict, because quoting spends against the co-loading bound. The note names this coupling ("independent as constraints but coupled through this remedy") and states the residual cases: the snapshot route or a split by claim. A second tension sets "requires opening nothing" against the representativeness limit. The note concedes this limit instead of hiding it. The claim keeps one consistent form.

## Thinnest joints

The two `UNSUPPORTED` joints rank highest because each carries a section's conclusion, and the stated reason does not reach that conclusion. The first claims that the validator would have caught findings it is not built to detect. The second reaches N-as-convention by elimination over an unproven set of three, then justifies it by an unlinked measurement. The three `THIN` joints are real but narrower. The loud-versus-silent comparison holds against the review-side policy the note describes, but not against review-side placement in general. The "prices already paid" claim is half-supported. The corpus demonstration is plausible but depends on quoting status and on a threshold the note leaves open. The co-loading bound, the check-relativity framing and the Descartes and Lamport precedents hold. The note explicitly limits the precedents to analogy.

## For the human
Look first at the reading of the paired experiment (lines 131–140). Decide whether a rule requiring quotes for attributed details exists or is being proposed. Without one, the claim that these absences are "a validator's result" has nothing beneath it.

# Critique: A note is an atomic step relative to the check that reads it

**Note:** kb/theory/a-note-is-an-atomic-step-relative-to-the-check-that-reads-it.md
**Central commitment:** A note's step size is relative to the check that reads it. For Commonplace's grounding check the unit is the unquoted source. Bounding that count on the artifact avoids the silent-failure mode of a review-side reading budget, because a conforming note fits the check by construction.
**Critique mode:** claim
**Attack outcome:** partially lands

## Strongest case against it

The opponent is the maintainer who holds the current review-side placement (ADR 079's sixteen-artifact budget), argued from measurement. Their case runs as follows.

The relativity claim and the two-bounds distinction are sound and not in dispute. The dispute is over the claim that matters operationally: that an artifact-side bound "does not have that failure mode". That claim does not survive. The bound counts unquoted sources. That count measures only the *finding* step the verbatim validator mechanizes. It does not measure the grounding check's actual cost. The remaining cost still needs off-page reading, and conformance does not shrink it:

1. **Representativeness.** A short verbatim passage can pass the substring validator while a qualifying sentence sits just outside it. The note says so itself: "a reader who suspects a passage was lifted out of a qualifying context has to open the source after all."
2. **Linked-note representation.** The unit excludes links to other notes on the grounds that each linked note discharges its own grounding. But the citing note still owes a faithful *representation*, and checking that means opening the linked note. In the paired experiment, one of the four uncapped-only findings was exactly this: "broader mechanism attributed to a link that disclaims it". No source-count bound would have touched it.
3. **Inference labelling.** Another of the four findings ("two target-side transfers not marked as hypotheses") was neither missing support nor a quote problem. It was a judgment about how the note frames its own inference.
4. **Absence detection.** The note says an absent retained passage "is a validator's result rather than a reviewer's finding." The validator it cites matches quotations that exist. It cannot report a quotation that should exist and doesn't. Noticing that absence was the uncapped reviewer's work.

So on a conforming note the reviewer's limit *can* still bind: whenever any of these four reasons sends the reviewer off the page. When it binds, the failure is just as silent as before. The artifact-side bound reduces how often the reviewer must leave the page. It does not remove the failure mode. Meanwhile the review-side budget, with consumption telemetry and sufficiency/budget disclosure, has a measured record: in the 68-note recertification, 37 of the 38 partial reads reported sufficiency, and the one budget stop named its unchecked routes. The opponent concludes that the note's own evidence supports both mechanisms as complements: the artifact bound cuts finding cost, and the review budget covers the residue. It does not support the artifact bound as a replacement free of the review budget's failure mode.

## How the note engages it

**Partially engaged.**

- *Representativeness* is answered directly in "Mechanism" ("Occurrence is not representativeness…") and in "What kind of number a step size is" ("the audit the bound buys is of the step the validator did not do, not of the one it cannot"). This part of the attack is already conceded and priced.
- *Linked-note representation* is raised as the first Open Question, which cites the very finding. The note therefore knows the residue exists. But the experiment section still reads the four findings as evidence that "the notes had put their support beyond" the cap. It never says that one of the four lies outside the proposed unit.
- *Inference labelling* is not engaged. The note recruits two of the four findings and is silent about the other two.
- *Absence detection* is not engaged. The note asserts the opposite of what its cited validator can do, and supports it with a counterfactual ("Had the details been quoted…") that presupposes an enforcement rule the Scope section explicitly leaves undecided.
- The *failure-mode* sentence in "Placing the bound on the artifact rather than the review" is stated without qualification ("on a conforming note it never binds"). This conflicts with the note's later concessions.

The attack does not reach the note's core: step size relative to the check, the two bounds coming apart, quoting jointly-supporting passages rather than splitting, and N as an auditability convention. These stand, and the note's precedents and scope bounds support them. The attack lands on the placement comparison and on how the note reads its own evidence.

## Constructive findings

- Qualify the failure-mode claim to what the validator actually removes. For example: the artifact-side bound removes the silent failure *for the finding step*. The reviewer's limit can still bind on representativeness, on linked-note representation and on inference framing, and those still need disclosure. This makes the placement section consistent with "Occurrence is not representativeness" and the first Open Question.
- Correct the "validator's result" sentence. Either name the missing enforcement rule as a premise (every source-attributed detail carries a verbatim quote or a `(snapshot required)` mark, checked mechanically), or describe the absence as a reviewer finding that the bound makes cheaper to reach.
- In the experiment paragraph, account for all four findings. Two are absences of retained support (in scope). One is a linked-note representation failure (outside the unit by construction). One is inference labelling (outside the unit). The evidence then supports what the note can actually claim: the artifact bound would have caught half the cap-hidden findings before review, and the rest still need a reviewer who reads.
- Mark the artifact-side side of the comparison as proposed rather than deployed, since its validator rule is not yet decided.

## Secondary objections (optional)

- The experiment counted "distinct linked artifacts", including linked notes and ingests. The note's unit is the unquoted source. The "six, eleven, fourteen and sixteen artifacts" figures are therefore not counts in the note's own unit. A reader could take them as showing those notes exceeded a source bound that was never measured.
- The corpus section counts notes in `kb/notes/` as of 2026-08-27, while the note itself lives in `kb/theory/`. If the collection has since moved, the location should be marked as historical so the count stays reproducible.

# Premise decomposition: A note is an atomic step relative to the check that reads it

**Register:** claim
**Central commitment (one sentence):** Notes are bounded twice, independently: once by co-loading and once by checking. The checking bound is relative to a named check, and for Commonplace's grounding check its unit is the unquoted source, which makes the bound placeable on the artifact rather than as a review-side reading budget.

## Premises and counterexamples

The commitment has three parts, and each consumes different premises.

1. **Two bounds, independent:** that the two quantities differ, and that size is meaningful only relative to a check. These premises hold. The note itself already prices the coupling through quoting.
2. **The unit is the unquoted source.** This part depends on three premises:
   - quoting a source removes it from the reviewer's work;
   - links to notes discharge their own grounding;
   - an absent passage is mechanically detectable.

   The pressure falls here. The paired assay the note relies on contains a partly quoted source whose unquoted details still required opening the source. That case defeats the source-level unit and points to a finer one: the unquoted attribution. The other two premises are dented by the same assay record and by the scope of the ADR 046 validator, which checks only quotes that are present.
3. **Artifact-side placement is better:** that a validator-held bound has no silent-failure mode, that the assay's four misses are about note size, and that N cannot be a capacity threshold. Each of these is stated more broadly than its support:
   - the silent-failure mode moves to the author's choice of passage;
   - two of the four misses are not about source placement;
   - "no observed loss" was not measurable in that design.

None of the failures propagates to the central commitment. Every one can be repaired by restating the unit more finely or by narrowing a reading of the evidence, so all are LOCAL. The auditability argument for a conventional N stands on its own and does not need the capacity premise.

## For the human

Look first at the DEFEATED unit premise. "A source that has been quoted verbatim is not one of them" fails on a partly quoted source, as in the compounding note's HyperAgents FAIL. Restating the unit as the unquoted attribution changes the Mechanism section, the description, and what any enforcing validator would have to count.

# Simplification synthesis: A note is an atomic step relative to the check that reads it

The note's central claim is clear and well placed: a note is bounded twice, and the checking bound is relative to a named check. For the grounding check, its unit is the unquoted source. None of the four checks found a buried thesis. The three opportunities below each combine several local findings into one structural change. Two remaining findings stay local and are not included: the thesis sentence that runs into two inline links, and the first Scope bullet that repeats the opening's scope sentence. Each can be fixed with a wording edit.

## Opportunities

### 1. Compress the precedent section to the precedent that does the work

- Location: "What kind of number a step size is", from "Sizing a step to its checker rather than to the material is old." to "...into a check that costs the reviewer nothing."
- Reader problem: Two paragraphs and five quotations support a point the note explicitly calls analogy, not evidence. The Descartes half also undercuts the point it is cited for. In the note's own gloss, "The parts are sized to the solution", and that is a different axis from sizing by checker. The reader spends attention there while the argument stands still.
- Direction: Keep one compact paragraph that states that checker-relative sizing has precedent. Use Lamport's "depends on the sophistication of the reader" as the main quotation, keep the analogy disclaimer, and end on the validator point ("What the knowledge-base case adds..."). One possible resolution: reduce Descartes to a single lineage clause, or move it to a separate lineage note.
- Combines: branch-bloat (Descartes as the weakest-fitting branch); detail-overhang WARN (precedents out of proportion to their job).
- Preserve or decide: Decide whether Descartes' "long chains of simple and easy reasonings" is part of the note's contribution. Keep it if the note means that reliable chains rest on simple links, because that connects to "Title as claim enables traversal as reasoning". Drop it if it is only historical colour. Preserve the analogy disclaimer, which blocks the inference that a particular N carries over. Lamport's "possible, not inevitable" currently supports the sentence "a bounded check does not catch every error, but an unbounded one cannot be redone". If that quotation is cut, the sentence must stand on the auditability argument alone, or move there.

### 2. Make the coupling of the two bounds a visible qualification of the opening

- Location: "Mechanism" section, the joint-support paragraph ("A consequence worth stating..." through "...owes representation, not re-grounding"), with the opening sentence "for two reasons that have nothing to do with each other" and the second Open Question.
- Reader problem: The opening says the bounds are unrelated. The only place the note qualifies that is one sentence in a paragraph that also recounts an archived proposal and makes an unrelated point about links. The second Open Question then asks about this paragraph's cost as though the body had not stated it. A reader can leave believing the bounds are fully independent, or that the joint-support cost is unexamined.
- Direction: Split the paragraph. Keep the joint-support remedy and its coupling together. Move "Links to other notes are also not sources in this sense..." to the start of the mechanism section, where the counted unit is defined. Reduce the archived-proposal history to a short attribution. Narrow the second Open Question to what remains open, for example how often joint support exceeds a co-loadable note, or cut it. One possible resolution: let the opening sentence say "independent as constraints" so the later coupling reads as a promised qualification, not a reversal.
- Combines: core-claim-obscured (coupling buried in a three-point paragraph); detail-overhang (archived-proposal provenance); marginal-value-redundancy (the second Open Question repeats the body).
- Preserve or decide: Decide how strong the independence claim is meant to be. "Nothing to do with each other" (different mechanisms) and "coupled through this remedy" (quoting spends co-loading budget) are compatible only if independence is about what sets each bound, not about whether satisfying one affects the other. The revision must state that distinction, not erase either side. Preserve the by-claim split requirement and the snapshot fallback.

### 3. Give auditability its role in the placement argument

- Location: "Placing the bound on the artifact rather than the review" and "What kind of number a step size is", around "The value is not that the reviewer copes, but that the review becomes auditable".
- Reader problem: The note gives two reasons for small artifact-side steps in two distant sections. Early on, review-side budgets fail silently. Late, small steps make verdicts redoable. The second reason, which the note treats as the main value, arrives after the evidence section has shown reviewers coping, and is then slowed by a restatement of "Occurrence is not representativeness". A reader may keep the title claim but lose why it matters.
- Direction: Preview auditability in one sentence in the placement section. In the N section, replace the "lifted out of a qualifying context" caveat with a short pointer to the earlier limit. One possible resolution for the preview: "a bound on the artifact also keeps each verdict small enough to redo — the reason, developed below, that N is a convention rather than a capacity."
- Combines: core-claim-obscured (auditability appears late); marginal-value-redundancy and detail-overhang (repeated representativeness caveat).
- Preserve or decide: The author must decide what auditability argues for. As written, it justifies the kind of number N is (a convention for re-checkability). It is not explicitly a reason to prefer artifact-side over review-side placement, because the placement section says the two "differ in their failure mode, not in the constraint they express". If auditability is meant as a second placement argument, the note has to say why a review-side budget does not deliver it. If not, the preview should tie it to N only. Preserve the distinction that the audit covers the support judgment and not representativeness, at least as a pointer.

# Assessment: A note is an atomic step relative to the check that reads it

**Proposed purpose (operator named none):** Agents and maintainers who design or
operate Commonplace's grounding review should understand that a note's step size
is relative to the check that reads it, what the grounding check's cost unit is,
and why the bound is placed on the artifact, with the limits of that placement
stated where the claims are made.

**Decision: stop.** The highest-value changes are claim corrections, not text
passes. Three claims are wrong or unsupported as stated, and one of them is the
unit that ADR 082, its archived proposal and the linked-note-grounding note rely
on. The passes do not change claims, so none is recommended.

## What reads well

The opening separation of the co-loading bound from the checking bound, and the
check-relativity of atomicity, are clear, well linked and held by every depth 1
report (premise decomposition: HOLDS on both).

## Ranked changes (highest value against the purpose first)

1. **Restate the cost unit from "the unquoted source" to the unquoted
   attribution** (Mechanism section, description, Scope). Premise decomposition
   marks "A source that has been quoted verbatim is not one of them" DEFEATED:
   a partly quoted source with further unquoted attributions still has to be
   opened, and the linked paired assay records exactly that case (the
   HyperAgents FAIL). Cost: a claim change touching the unit dependents rely on.
   Pass: none — rewrite route.
2. **Correct "an absence of that kind is a validator's result rather than a
   reviewer's finding"** (experiment section). The ADR 046 validator matches
   quotes that exist; it cannot detect a missing quote. Flagged by composition
   friction (UNSUPPORTED), critique, premise decomposition, epistemic-status-blur,
   grounding-alignment and framing-mismatch. Either name a required-quote rule
   as a premise or restate the absence as a reviewer finding the bound makes
   cheaper. Cost: claim change. Pass: none — rewrite route.
3. **Qualify "An artifact-side bound does not have that failure mode … on a
   conforming note it never binds"** (placement section). The silent failure
   moves to the author's choice of passage, to linked-note representation and
   to inference labelling; the note concedes some of this later but not here.
   Critique, friction and premise decomposition all attack it. Cost: claim
   narrowing on a passage ADR 082 relies on for placement. Pass: narrow-overclaims
   would fit the wording, but the narrowing changes the placement argument
   dependents use, so it goes to the operator.
4. **Account for all four cap-only findings in the experiment rereading.** Two
   (linked-note representation; unmarked hypotheses) fall outside the proposed
   unit; the note recruits only two and says "the four notes would have had to
   split or quote". Cost: evidence reinterpretation. Pass: none — rewrite route.
5. **Weaken "no observed loss … not a reviewer capacity exhausted"**. The assay
   had no ground truth for misses in PASS outcomes and the linked report
   declines that conclusion (grounding-alignment, epistemic-status-blur, premise
   decomposition). Cost: two-sentence narrowing. Pass: narrow-overclaims, but
   held with the rest of the rewrite.
6. **Specify the corpus count's population and unit** ("eight cite more than
   five distinct sources"): distinct sources vs unquoted sources, and `kb/notes/`
   vs the note's own `kb/theory/` location; no method or link. Cost: evidence
   restatement; the count is duplicated in the linked-note-grounding note.
   Pass: none — claim question.
7. Text-level work that would follow a rewrite: compress the Descartes/Lamport
   precedent section (detail-overhang, synthesis opportunity 1; the Descartes
   gloss also sizes parts to the solution, not the checker); surface the
   bound coupling and soften "nothing to do with each other" (synthesis 2,
   internal-consistency); place auditability in the placement argument
   (synthesis 3); define N and gloss "ingest" and "snapshot"; split the packed
   oracle-domain sentence and the archived-proposal appositive; fix "the one it
   cannot", "which is the behaviour…", "prices already paid elsewhere"; the
   title/body alignment ("Whether a note is an atomic step depends on…").
   Pass: abstractions, readability-and-flow, plain-wording, opening-and-title,
   fix-strategy-taxonomy. Not recommended now: a rewrite will replace much of
   this text.

## Sentence a hostile reviewer attacks first

"Both are absences of a retained passage, and an absence of that kind is a
validator's result rather than a reviewer's finding." It asserts a capability
the cited validator lacks, and the section's reinterpretation of the experiment
rests on it.

## Overclaim candidates: support or divergence

- "A step is atomic relative to a particular check" — divergence (keep).
- "These are different quantities set by different mechanisms, and a note can
  satisfy one and fail the other." — divergence (keep).
- "N is a convention, chosen so that a second checker — including a person —
  can redo the step." — divergence (keep; premise decomposition HOLDS; friction
  calls the elimination over three candidates thin, which may be narrowed).
- "An artifact-side bound does not have that failure mode" — support (narrow).
- "an absence of that kind is a validator's result" — support (correct).
- "on this evidence it is not a reviewer capacity exhausted" — support (narrow).
- "under such a bound the four notes would have had to split or quote" —
  support (narrow to the two source-retention findings).

## Stale qualifications (claim questions for the operator)

- Scope says the note "Does not decide N, a validator rule that would enforce
  it, or the fate of the review-side budget currently in force", and the footer
  calls ADR 079 "currently in force". The role report says ADR 082, accepted and
  resting on this note, decides five sources with a FAIL rule and drops the
  reader-side caps. The present-tense validator in the placement section and
  the "hypothetical validator" objections from critique and friction both turn
  on this status.
- The corpus count is scoped to `kb/notes/` as of 2026-08-27, while the note
  now lives in `kb/theory/`.
- The archived proposal *Exceeding a review budget splits the task* and the
  self-disagreement measurement are cited without links (orphan-references).

`kb/reports/state/review/runs/v2/revise/kb/theory/a-note-is-an-atomic-step-relative-to-the-check-that-reads-it/0ab4dcfcce1b/role`.
The unit ("the unquoted source", with quoted sources and linked notes exempt)

and `kb/theory/a-linked-note-discharges-its-own-grounding-so-a-citing-note-owes.md`
(which also carries the 344/eight corpus count). Restating the unit as the
unquoted attribution changes what ADR 082's validator must count.

## Findings not acted on, with reasons

All fourteen stored findings are deferred by the stop; none is planned because
the rewrite will replace or move the passages they name.

- `semantic/epistemic-status-blur`, `semantic/grounding-alignment`,
  `sentence/framing-mismatch`: their main findings are the claim errors in

- `semantic/internal-consistency`: "costs the reviewer nothing" contradicts the
  body's support-judgment cost; a claim-level fix tied to item 1.
- `semantic/underspecified-assertions`, `prose/orphan-references`: corpus-count
  population and unlinked measurements; claim/evidence questions (item 6).
- `frontmatter/title-body-alignment`: a title change on a note whose title

- `compression-bundle/detail-overhang`, `compression-bundle/marginal-value-redundancy`,
  `accessibility/notation-opacity`, `accessibility/undefined-terms`,
  `prose/mannered-prose`, `sentence/clause-packing`, `sentence/parsing-ambiguity`:
  valid text-level fixes on passages a rewrite is expected to change; rerun the
